purpose: Pyrimethamine is used to treat and prevent certain parasitic infections, most commonly toxoplasmosis and malaria. It is often combined with other medicines to work more effectively. It is especially important for people with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS.
how_it_works: Pyrimethamine works by blocking a key process that parasites need to grow and reproduce — specifically, it stops them from making folate, which is like a vitamin they need to survive. Without folate, the parasites cannot multiply and eventually die off. Your own body cells handle this differently, so the medicine targets the parasites more than it affects you.
common_side_effects: You may notice nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, or a sore tongue. Some people develop skin rashes or feel unusually tired. Over time, it can lower your blood cell counts, which may make you feel weak or more prone to infections or bruising.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious decreases in your blood counts, so your doctor will do regular blood tests while you are on it. Because it affects folate in your body, you will likely be given a supplement called leucovorin (folinic acid) to help protect your blood cells. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bruising, bleeding, fever, or signs of infection. Pregnant women should use this medicine only if clearly needed, as it may affect the developing baby.
typical_dosing: Dosing varies a lot depending on what condition is being treated. For toxoplasmosis, a common starting dose for adults is 200 mg on the first day, then 50 to 75 mg daily along with other medicines. For malaria prevention, lower doses are used. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions, as your dose will be tailored specifically to your needs.
